entries.name: Mission-Born Christianity in New France
entries.placeLabel: Quebec · the Huron country and beyond
entries.statusWord: Researched — on the atlas, no convert voice yet
entries.statusDescription: The Jesuits' yearly Relations are in hand, in French and English, to 1650. The converts speak in them only as the missionaries wrote them down; no text in a convert's own hand is in the Library yet. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Rich on the mission side, and one-sided. The Jesuits' yearly reports, the Relations, are in hand to 1650, in French with English beside it. The converts are heard only through the missionaries. Their speeches come to us as the priests wrote them down, for readers in France. No text in a convert's own hand is in the Library yet.
entries.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question is how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
entries.relationsSummary: Grew from the Jesuit mission to New France. Near Quebec, Algonquin families settled at Sillery from 1638, and most became Christians. Far to the west, the Jesuits worked among the Hurons. When war with the Iroquois broke the Huron nation, about three hundred Christian Hurons went down to Quebec in 1650.
entries.why: Here the converts' words survive, though only in the priests' reports. At Sillery, Christian families met at night without the Jesuits and made rules of their own. Among the Hurons, a convert named Joseph Chihwatenhwa taught his people like an elder brother. In 1650 the last Huron Christians asked to be led to Quebec, so that their faith would not die out.
entries.teaser: Quebec and the Huron country, 1610 to 1650: Algonquin and Huron Christians, heard only through the Jesuits who wrote them down.
entries.longDescription:
On 24 June 1610 a chief named Membertou was baptized at Port Royal in Acadia. About twenty of his family and people were baptized with him. A French priest named Fléché baptized them, about a year before the first Jesuits came. The first report in the Jesuit Relations collection is from that year.

Near Quebec, the Jesuits set up a settlement at Sillery in 1637 and 1638. One evening a man named Negabamat came to hold Father Le Jeune to his word. Had he not promised a house for him and another family? Two Algonquin families settled there, and within a year most of the settlers were Christians. Negabamat took the name Noël.

In 1640 the Christians of Sillery met at night, with no priest present. Negabamat told the others that the French taught that "we all are brothers". An old captain, Jean Baptiste Etinechkavat, said he had weighed the faith well before he took it. One man who was not baptized spoke against them. He would not give up the old right to take more than one wife.

The same Christians agreed among themselves that anyone who sinned should be jailed and made to fast. They told the Jesuits only the next morning. The priests said they were too severe, but the converts kept to their plan. Charles Meiachkawat, just baptized, told them to bind him if he ever lost courage.

Among the Hurons, Joseph Chihwatenhwa was for months the only Christian in his village, with his family. His people spoke hard words against him. The Jesuits called him "Our Christian" and wrote down his speeches. In the summer of 1640 he was killed while he worked in his field. The Jesuit report says two Iroquois killed him.

By 1650, war with the Iroquois had broken the Huron nation. The survivors gathered on the Island of Saint Joseph. There two old captains came in secret to the Jesuit superior. "More than ten thousand have been snatched away by death," they told him. They asked him to lead the rest to Quebec. "There, our faith will not die out," they said. About three hundred went down to Quebec with the Jesuits that year.

Every word of theirs comes to us through the Jesuits. The priests wrote each year for readers in France, to build them up in faith. What the converts meant, and what they doubted, we see only through those reports.
voices: Membertou — a chief at Port Royal in Acadia, baptized with about twenty of his family and people on 24 June 1610
Noël Negabamat — one of the first settlers at Sillery, whose speeches of 1638 and 1640 Father Le Jeune wrote down
Jean Baptiste Etinechkavat — a captain at Sillery, who said in 1640 that he had weighed the faith well before he took it
Charles Meiachkawat — newly baptized at Sillery in 1640, who told the others to bind him if he ever lost courage
Joseph Chihwatenhwa — for months the only Christian in his Huron village; killed in his field in 1640
entries.legacy: The Library's record of this church stops in 1650. A year before, the Jesuits counted more than three thousand people baptized among the Hurons. The few hundred who reached Quebec had lost their homes and their kin. The Jesuit who led them wrote that they "have not lost their faith." What became of their church after 1650 is not yet told from the Library.

livingEvidence.basis: The Library's last word is the move of about three hundred Huron Christians to Quebec in 1650. No text in the repo traces a church descended from them after that year.

entries.name: The Swedish Lutherans of New Sweden
entries.informalName: The Swedish Congregations on the Delaware
entries.region: The Delaware River: Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed. Thin: one source, Acrelius (1759).
entries.sourcing: Thin: one source. Israel Acrelius, the Swedish provost on the Delaware, wrote this history, printed in 1759. He copied in the people's own letters, such as their plea of 1693 for ministers and books. Acrelius's own account stops in 1756, when he went home. Only his editor's notes of 1874 carry the story on to 1786. No church book or other record of the congregations is in the Library yet.
entries.floorNote: No question. They held to what their own letter of 1693 called "the pure and uncorrupted Lutheran religion".
entries.relationsSummary: Sweden planted a colony on the Delaware in 1638, with a Swedish pastor. After Swedish rule ended in 1655, few pastors were left. In 1693 the people wrote home to beg for ministers and books. From 1697 the king and archbishop of Sweden sent pastors again. In the 1740s the churches shut out Moravian preachers. Their provost Acrelius visited the cloister at Ephrata in 1753 and argued with its brothers.
entries.why: A small Swedish people on an American river kept their Lutheran church for more than a century. For years they had no pastor of their own tongue. Laymen read sermons from a book in the churches. In 1693 they wrote to Sweden in their own words, for "two Swedish ministers" and two hundred catechisms. Sweden answered, and went on sending pastors for nearly ninety years.
entries.teaser: The Delaware River, 1638 to 1786: Swedish farmers who kept their own church and begged home for pastors and books.
entries.longDescription:
In 1638 Swedish settlers built Fort Christina on the Delaware River. Their pastor, Reorus Torkillus, came from East Gothland in Sweden. The colony stayed small, and its churches were built of logs.

Swedish rule ended in 1655, and one Swedish pastor, Lars Lock, stayed on. In 1677 the people called a second pastor, Jacob Fabritius, who preached in Dutch. By 1691 he was too old to serve. Then, Acrelius writes, an old man read sermons out of a book in one church, and Charles Springer read in another. "The people waited, but no clergyman came."

Springer had a strange road to the river. He was seized in London, shipped to America and sold as a servant in Virginia. Once free, he joined his own people on the Delaware. In 1693 he wrote for them to Sweden. They asked for "two Swedish ministers", for Bibles, and for two hundred catechisms. They were farmers, they said, who lived "according to the laudable old Swedish customs". They were ready to seal their faith "with our own blood".

The letter reached King Charles XI. In 1697 three pastors arrived with a commission from the king and the archbishop. The people built two brick and stone churches. Trinity Church at Christina was consecrated in 1699, and Gloria Dei at Wicaco in 1700.

In the 1740s Moravian preachers came among the Swedes. In 1744 one of them, Bruzelius, was set to preach at Raccoon church. His opponents held the key, so his friends broke in through a window. A panel of twenty-five men later ruled against him. Moravian ministers were then barred from the Swedish and English churches.

Acrelius came as provost in 1749 and went home in 1756. He urged the people to keep the Swedish language and teach it to the young. Yet the English tongue was gaining, and some services were already held in English.
voices: Charles Springer — kidnapped in London and sold as a servant in Virginia, he became a reader and church warden among the Swedes and wrote their letter of 1693 to Sweden
Israel Acrelius — provost of the Swedish churches on the Delaware from 1749 to 1756, whose history of the congregations was printed in 1759
entries.legacy: From 1696 to 1786, Sweden sent twenty-four pastors to the churches on the Delaware. The crown paid for their voyages out and home. In time the Swedish language died out among the settlers' children. Then Sweden stopped sending pastors. What became of the congregations after that is not yet told from the Library.

entries.name: English Unitarianism
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as a register entry. By its own founding sermon and writings, it reads as stepping outside the doctrinal floor. The question is not decided yet. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Moderate. The Library holds Lindsey's sermon at the opening of his chapel in 1774, and Priestley's own memoir to 1795. It holds Priestley's open letters to the New Church of 1791, and a New Church reply. Belsham's account of 1812, from his life of Lindsey, is here too. Biddle's English life of Socinus, printed in London in 1653, is here too. Toulmin's own books are named but not yet in hand. Nye, named among the early English Unitarians, is not yet in the Library, so this entry says nothing of what he wrote.
entries.floorNote: Lindsey's chapel was formed so that its people might worship "God alone", the Father. Priestley defended "the unitarian doctrine" in print every year. By their own account, they did not hold the Trinity. This is their own account, not a charge made by their opponents. Whether it places them outside the floor is not yet decided.
entries.relationsSummary: Theophilus Lindsey left the Church of England. In 1774 he opened his own chapel in London. Joseph Priestley came to it from the old Dissenting churches. There he had moved from Arian to Unitarian belief. Earlier English writers took up the ideas of Socinus and the Polish Brethren. The evidence for that link is thin. Lindsey's prayer book shaped the first Unitarian liturgy in Boston. Priestley argued in print with the new Swedenborgian church in Birmingham. One of its leaders answered him.
entries.why: In 1774 a clergyman who had left the Church of England opened a chapel in London. Its people met, he said, as "a separate congregation", so that they might worship God alone. Joseph Priestley, chemist and Dissenting minister, defended the same belief in print each year. In 1791 a mob burned his meeting house and his home in Birmingham. In 1813 the law at last gave Unitarians the same rights as other Dissenters.
entries.teaser: London and Birmingham, 1774 to 1813: a chapel built to worship God alone, and a minister whose church was burned.
entries.longDescription:
Theophilus Lindsey was a Church of England clergyman at Catterick, in Yorkshire. He grew uneasy in his post and thought of leaving it. Others in that church were trying to end the rule that clergy must sign its Thirty-Nine Articles. Lindsey left, and on 17 April 1774 he opened a chapel in Essex Street, in London.

In his first sermon there, Lindsey said why they had come together. They were "a separate congregation, distinct from that of our national church". They met so that they "may be at liberty to worship God alone". No one, he said, should make others sign his own reading of Scripture. The prayers that day spoke to the Father: "thou art God alone".

Joseph Priestley came from the other side, the old Dissent. He and his fellow tutors at a Dissenting academy, he wrote, "were likewise all Arians". At Leeds he became what was called a Socinian, holding that Christ was a man and not God. In London he spent his Sundays at Lindsey's chapel and sometimes led its worship. He wrote a pamphlet every year in defence of "the unitarian doctrine".

In Birmingham, Priestley also argued with the new Swedenborgian church. His letters of 1791 rejected its teaching that the one God is Jesus Christ. Robert Hindmarsh, a leader of that church, answered him in 1792. A Socinian, he wrote, had no right to the name of a Christian.

On 14 July 1791 a mob in Birmingham burned the church where Priestley preached. Then they burned his home. It wrecked the houses of many Dissenters too. Priestley moved to Hackney, near London. A church there asked him to be its minister. In April 1794 he sailed for America. Thomas Belsham taught at the college in Hackney. He later served the Essex Street chapel.

The same belief had English voices long before Lindsey. In 1653 John Biddle put a life of Socinus, the Polish Brethren's teacher, into English. In 1777 Joshua Toulmin, a Baptist pastor at Taunton, wrote a new life of Socinus. A Baptist editor wrote in 1910 that some Baptist churches in the west of England turned Unitarian too.

The chapel's prayer book crossed the sea. In 1786 the minister of King's Chapel in Boston wrote to Lindsey about his new liturgy. He said he had tried to bring in Lindsey's whole liturgy. He also credited Lindsey's books for the spread of Unitarian belief in New England.
voices: Theophilus Lindsey — left the Church of England and opened the Essex Street chapel in London on 17 April 1774
Joseph Priestley — chemist and Dissenting minister, who wrote a pamphlet each year for the Unitarian belief; his Birmingham meeting house and home were burned in 1791
Thomas Belsham — divinity tutor at Hackney and later of Essex Street, whose life of Lindsey (1812) tells the movement's story
Joshua Toulmin — Baptist minister at Taunton, who wrote a life of Socinus in 1777
John Biddle — who put a life of Socinus into English in 1653, an early English voice for the same belief
entries.legacy: For years Unitarians stood outside the law that protected other Dissenters. In 1813 they were given the same rights. By then the chapel's books were read far from London. In 1810 a small society in New York State read sermons by Lindsey, Priestley and Toulmin when it had no minister. The story of the English churches after 1813 is not yet told from the Library.

livingEvidence.basis: The Library carries the Essex Street chapel to Belsham's account of 1812 and the law of 1813. No later text in the repo traces today's British Unitarian churches back to it.
